lead: SONET in North America and SDH elsewhere define one synchronous frame that carries many low-rate channels on a single optical line. One master clock and byte interleaving let any channel be added or dropped without splitting the whole signal. The frame repeats every 125 μs, so rates are exact multiples of 51.84 Mb/s. Telephone companies use these networks for voice, leased lines and protected rings; data networks use them as a reliable pipe under packet traffic.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for the wavelength layer and Unit 3 for why electronics cannot simply run at the line rate.

blocks.text: Early plesiochronous multiplexers gave every channel its own clock. To add one 2 Mb/s telephone line, the operator demultiplexed the high-rate signal down to that line and rebuilt everything. SONET (North America) and SDH (Europe and most of the world) replace this with one synchronous frame. All nodes lock to a primary reference clock, and bytes from many channels are interleaved in fixed positions.

The basic SONET rate is OC-1 = 51.84 Mb/s. Higher rates are exact multiples: OC-n = n × 51.84 Mb/s. SDH uses STM-1 = 155.52 Mb/s = OC-3. The table gives the common steps; the optical line rate is slightly higher than the payload because overhead bytes are added at every layer.

A pointer in the line overhead marks where the synchronous payload envelope (SPE) starts inside the frame. If a node's clock runs slightly fast or slow, the pointer moves by one byte and a stuffing byte is added or removed. The payload therefore floats without a slip. Concatenation, written STS-3c, ties three STS-1 payloads into one container with one pointer; STM-1/VC-4 does the same job in SDH.

The frame is a rectangle: 90 columns × 9 rows = 810 bytes. It lasts 125 μs, so 8000 frames pass per second. Of the 90 columns, 3 are transport overhead: section and line. The other 87 columns form the SPE; the first column of the SPE is path overhead. The SPE is 87 × 9 = 783 bytes. The pointer bytes H1, H2 and H3 are in the transport overhead, never in the payload.

blocks.where: R is the STS-1 line rate; 810 is bytes per frame, 8 bits per byte, and 8000 frames per second.

blocks.text: For STS-1 the SPE rate is 50.112 Mb/s. This envelope includes path overhead and fixed stuff; the user payload is 48.384 Mb/s. An STM-1 carries a VC-4 with 149.76 Mb/s payload capacity. An OC-3 frame is not 810 bytes: it is three interleaved STS-1 frames, 2430 bytes, in the same 125 μs.

SONET/SDH is divided into layers. The section layer runs between regenerators and monitors framing and section error bytes. The line layer runs between add-drop multiplexers, carries the pointer and protection signalling, and monitors line errors. The path layer runs end to end between the nodes that create and read the payload; it monitors path errors and the path trace. Each layer checks its own overhead, so a fault can be located without taking the whole signal apart.

An add-drop multiplexer (ADM) uses byte positions. It drops selected columns, inserts new traffic into the same positions, and passes the rest. It does not need to demultiplex every channel. In a UPSR (unidirectional path switched ring) or SDH SNCP, the signal is bridged on both directions and the receiver selects the better copy. In a BLSR (bidirectional line switched ring) or MS-SPRing, protection capacity is shared and working traffic loops back at a failure. Both are designed to restore within 50 ms.
Jitter is short-term phase variation, above about 10 Hz. Wander is slow phase drift, below about 10 Hz. Pointers absorb wander; interface specifications limit jitter.

examples.question: An STS-1 frame is 810 bytes and repeats 8000 times per second. (a) Find the bit rate. (b) Find the SPE rate for the 783-byte envelope. (c) What fraction of the frame is transport overhead outside the SPE? (d) How many 2.048 Mb/s E1 signals does one STM-1 carry if they are packed 3 × 7 × 3? Give the carried E1 bit rate.
steps: (a) Bits per frame = 810 × 8 = 6480 bits. Line rate = 6480 × 8000 = 51,840,000 b/s = 51.84 Mb/s.
(b) SPE bits per frame = 783 × 8 = 6264 bits. SPE rate = 6264 × 8000 = 50,112,000 b/s = 50.112 Mb/s.
(c) Transport overhead bytes = 810 − 783 = 27 bytes. Fraction = 27 ÷ 810 = 0.03333 = 3.33 percent.
(d) E1 count = 3 × 7 × 3 = 63 E1s. Carried rate = 63 × 2.048 = 129.024 Mb/s. The VC-4 payload is 149.76 Mb/s, so the rest is overhead and stuffing.
examples.answer: The line rate is 51.84 Mb/s, the SPE rate is 50.112 Mb/s, transport overhead is 3.33 percent, and one STM-1 carries 63 E1s at 129.024 Mb/s.
examples.check:
frame = 810
spe = 783
fps = 8000
bits = 8
line_rate = frame * bits * fps
spe_rate = spe * bits * fps
overhead = (frame - spe) / frame * 100
e1 = 3 * 7 * 3
e1_rate = e1 * 2.048
print(round(line_rate / 1e6, 3))
print(round(spe_rate / 1e6, 3))
print(round(overhead, 2))
print(e1)
print(round(e1_rate, 3))

traps: The 810-byte frame belongs to STS-1/OC-1. An OC-3 frame is three interleaved STS-1 frames, 2430 bytes, not 810 bytes.
Do not divide 155.52 Mb/s by 2.048 Mb/s to count E1s. The SDH multiplex is 3 × 7 × 3 = 63 E1s in STM-1; the rest is overhead and stuffing.
Pointer bytes H1, H2 and H3 sit in the transport overhead, not inside the SPE. They mark the start of the floating envelope.
The 810 − 783 = 27 bytes are transport overhead only. The 783-byte SPE still contains path overhead; total overhead including path overhead is 36 bytes, or 4.44 percent.
UPSR/SNCP sends the signal along both directions and selects; BLSR/MS-SPRing loops back and shares protection capacity. Do not swap the two.

quiz.q: State the OC-3 line rate and its SDH name.
Why does a synchronous frame use pointers?
quiz.a: Pointers let the SPE float inside the frame so small clock differences are absorbed by a pointer move and stuffing, without demultiplexing the payload.

quiz.q: An STS-1 frame has 3 columns of transport overhead and 1 column of path overhead out of 90 columns. Find the SPE bytes and the SPE rate at 8000 frames per second.
quiz.a: SPE columns = 90 − 3 = 87. SPE bytes = 87 × 9 = 783. SPE rate = 783 × 8 × 8000 = 50.112 Mb/s.

quiz.q: An STM-1 carries 63 E1s packed 3 × 7 × 3. Explain why the E1 rate is below 155.52 Mb/s.
quiz.a: 63 × 2.048 = 129.024 Mb/s. The rest is STM-1/SDH transport and path overhead, plus VC-12/TU pointers and stuffing. The VC-4 payload is 149.76 Mb/s.

quiz.q: How many OC-12 equivalents fit in one OC-48 line?
quiz.a: OC-48 ÷ OC-12 = 48 ÷ 12 = 4. OC-48 equals four OC-12 lines.

quiz.q: A ring must survive one fiber cut within 50 ms. Compare UPSR and BLSR.
quiz.a: UPSR bridges the path on both directions and the receiver selects; no re-route is needed. BLSR loops working traffic onto shared protection capacity, so it uses fiber capacity better. Both are designed for sub-50 ms protection.

quiz.q: What does the section layer monitor?
quiz.a: The section layer monitors framing and section error bytes between regenerators.

beyond: Not for the exam. SONET/SDH is still present in metro, utility and railway networks because it gives hard QoS and fast protection. New high-rate systems use OTN (G.709), which wraps SONET/SDH and Ethernet into larger containers. Synchronous Ethernet and IEEE 1588 PTP distribute timing for packet networks, taking over the old master-clock role. Search OTN, GFP, SyncE and PTP.
